concepts.name: Immediate Triggers and Context of Quit India Movement
key_dimensions: Failure of Cripps Mission (March–April 1942) as the proximate cause
Fall of Singapore and Japanese advance threatening India's eastern borders
Deteriorating wartime economic conditions and peasant discontent
Gandhi's shift from 'non-embarrassment' policy to direct confrontation with British

concepts.name: Cripps Mission 1942: Proposals, Rejection and Significance
key_dimensions: Key proposals: Dominion Status after war, constituent assembly with princely states, right to secede from Commonwealth
Congress rejection: 'Post-dated cheque on a failing bank' (Gandhi's metaphor), no immediate transfer of power
Muslim League's rejection: Inadequate safeguards for Pakistan demand
Ambedkar's and other minorities' positions on the Cripps proposals
Role of Cripps Mission failure in making Quit India inevitable

concepts.name: Wardha Resolution and the 'Do or Die' Call
key_dimensions: Wardha Working Committee Resolution (July 14, 1942): ideological foundation of QIM
'Do or Die' slogan — context, meaning, and Gandhi's intent vs. British interpretation
Debate within Congress: Nehru and Rajagopalachari's initial reservations vs. Gandhi's insistence
Distinction between Gandhi's 'orderly withdrawal' demand and mass uprising that followed

concepts.name: AICC Bombay Session (August 8, 1942): Formal Launch
key_dimensions: Gowalia Tank (August Kranti Maidan) resolution — formal declaration
Gandhi's speech: Concept of 'non-violent army' and the role of every individual
Arrest of Congress leadership on August 9, 1942 — Operation Thunderbolt by British
Significance of pre-emptive British crackdown in shaping the leaderless character of the movement

concepts.name: Leaderless Nature of QIM: Spontaneous Mass Uprising
key_dimensions: Contrast with earlier movements (NCM, CDM) that were centrally controlled by Gandhi
Role of underground networks: Jayaprakash Narayan, Ram Manohar Lohia, Aruna Asaf Ali
'Do or Die' interpreted differently by masses vs. Gandhi's original non-violent vision
UPSC trap: QIM was NOT purely non-violent — widespread violence, sabotage of railways, telegraph lines

concepts.name: Role of Underground Leaders in QIM
key_dimensions: Jayaprakash Narayan: Escape from Hazaribagh jail, organizing underground Congress Radio
Aruna Asaf Ali: Hoisting Congress flag at Gowalia Tank; symbol of women's leadership
Ram Manohar Lohia: Underground radio broadcasts, 'Congress Radio' operations
Sucheta Kriplani and other women leaders — distinction from earlier movements
UPSC trap: Role of socialist faction within Congress (CSP members) dominating underground operations

concepts.name: Regional Epicentres: Satara, Midnapore, Ballia and Tamluk
key_dimensions: Satara (Maharashtra): 'Prati Sarkar' (parallel government) under Nana Patil — most sustained parallel government
Ballia (UP): Chittu Pandey led temporary expulsion of British administration
Tamluk (Midnapore, Bengal): 'Tamralipta Jatiya Sarkar' — parallel government with Matangini Hazra's role
UPSC trap: Distinguishing which parallel governments were short-lived vs. sustained (Satara most durable)
Significance of parallel governments as precursors to Gram Swaraj concept

concepts.name: British Response and Repression
key_dimensions: Mass arrests: Over 100,000 imprisoned including entire Congress leadership
Aerial bombing and machine-gunning of crowds — unprecedented in colonial history
Press censorship and collective fines on villages
Linlithgow's characterization: 'Most serious rebellion since 1857' — significance of this admission
Emergency powers invoked under Defence of India Rules

concepts.name: Muslim League and QIM: Position and Implications
key_dimensions: Muslim League's non-participation and cooperation with British war effort
Jinnah's characterization of QIM as 'Congress blackmail'
League's expansion during Congress absence (1942–45): Provincial recruitment, political consolidation
UPSC trap: QIM's indirect consequence — strengthening of Muslim League's bargaining position
Hindu Mahasabha and RSS also did not participate — broader non-participation pattern

concepts.name: Communist Party of India (CPI) and QIM: The Controversial Stance
key_dimensions: CPI's opposition to QIM — 'People's War' thesis after Germany attacked USSR (June 1941)
British government's decision to legalize CPI in 1942 as a result of its anti-QIM stance
Long-term damage to CPI's nationalist credentials and its relationship with Congress
UPSC trap: CPI was the ONLY major political party that actively opposed QIM and cooperated with British

concepts.name: Gandhi's Imprisonment and the Fast (1943)
key_dimensions: Gandhi imprisoned at Aga Khan Palace, Pune (August 1942 – May 1944)
21-day fast (February 1943): Protest against British allegations of Gandhi instigating violence
Deaths of Mahadev Desai and Kasturba Gandhi during this imprisonment
British refusal to negotiate — Linlithgow-Gandhi correspondence and its historical significance
UPSC trap: Gandhi's fast was NOT to end QIM but to protest British characterization of him

concepts.name: Role of Students and Youth in QIM
key_dimensions: Student strikes, boycott of educational institutions across provinces
All India Students Federation's role in mobilization
Youth participation distinguishing QIM from previous movements dominated by lawyers/merchants
Connection to post-war nationalist leadership emerging from QIM participants

concepts.name: Role of Women in QIM
key_dimensions: Aruna Asaf Ali as the most iconic female leader — 'Heroine of 1942'
Matangini Hazra (Bengal): Martyrdom, 'Vande Mataram' till death — symbol of peasant women's participation
Usha Mehta: Operation of Congress Radio from underground
QIM as a turning point in mass participation of ordinary women (not just elite women leaders)
UPSC trap: Distinguishing roles — Aruna Asaf Ali (urban underground) vs. Matangini Hazra (rural mass movement)

concepts.name: Parallel Governments (Pratinidhi Sabhas): Nature and Significance
key_dimensions: Ideological basis: Foreshadowing of Gandhi's village swaraj and decentralized governance
Satara Prati Sarkar: Functions — courts, police, education, revenue collection
Difference between Ballia (short-lived, 1 week) and Satara (1942–45, most sustained)
British inability to fully suppress — significance for understanding limits of colonial power
UPSC trap: These were NOT planned by Congress leadership but emerged spontaneously

concepts.name: Sabotage and Violence in QIM: Ideological Tensions
key_dimensions: Railway sabotage, telegraph cutting, post office attacks — systematic pattern
Gandhi's response: Neither endorsed nor condemned all violence equally
JP Narayan's 'Azad Dasta' (Free Brigade) — organized armed resistance wing
UPSC trap: QIM was NOT entirely non-violent — this is a frequently tested nuance
Debate among historians: Mass violence as spontaneous vs. organized (Gyanendra Pandey vs. official nationalist narrative)

concepts.name: Congress Radio (Underground Radio): Significance
key_dimensions: Operated by Usha Mehta from multiple locations in Bombay (August–November 1942)
Broadcast Congress messages, countered British propaganda, maintained movement morale
Eventually traced and shut down by British in November 1942
Significance: First use of radio as a tool of mass political resistance in Indian nationalism
UPSC trap: Usha Mehta operated Congress Radio, NOT Aruna Asaf Ali (common confusion)

concepts.name: QIM and Indian National Army (INA): Interconnection
key_dimensions: Parallel timing: INA's reorganization under Subhas Chandra Bose (1943) coincided with QIM suppression
QIM's failure pushing some revolutionaries toward INA/armed resistance path
British strategic concern: QIM + Japanese advance + INA = existential threat in 1942–43
UPSC trap: INA and QIM were SEPARATE movements with different strategies but shared anti-British goal
Significance of 1942 as the year multiple anti-British forces converged simultaneously

concepts.name: Historiographical Debates on QIM
key_dimensions: Nationalist interpretation: Decisive blow that made British quit India inevitable
Revisionist view (R.J. Moore, Francis Hutchins): QIM was suppressed; partition, not QIM, forced British withdrawal
Gyanendra Pandey: QIM as subaltern rebellion beyond Congress control
Sumit Sarkar's position: QIM as 'near-revolutionary' situation but ultimately contained
UPSC trap: Distinguishing between immediate failure (movement suppressed) and long-term success (psychological impact)

concepts.name: Consequences and Legacy of QIM
key_dimensions: Short-term: Movement suppressed by 1943, Congress leadership jailed till June 1945
Long-term: Demonstrated mass nationalist consciousness was irreversible
British realisation: Governing India post-war without Congress cooperation was impossible
Political consequence: Strengthened Muslim League and princely states' bargaining positions
UPSC trap: QIM did NOT directly cause British departure — it created conditions; actual transfer came after 1945 elections, INA trials, and RIN Mutiny

concepts.name: QIM vs. Earlier Gandhian Movements: Comparative Analysis
key_dimensions: Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22): Suspended after Chauri Chaura; centrally controlled
Civil Disobedience Movement (1930–34): Gandhi as sole commander; specific demands
QIM uniqueness: No suspension despite violence; leaderless; most radical demand (complete independence)
UPSC trap: QIM was the ONLY movement Gandhi did not suspend despite widespread violence
Comparison of British responses: Relative moderation in CDM vs. extreme repression in QIM
